cards.definition: A name that holds a value.
Text in quotes, such as "hello".
A whole number, such as 7 or -3.
A number with a decimal point, such as 2.5.
A value that is either True or False.
Many values kept in order, written with square brackets.
Values stored under names (keys), written with curly brackets.
A named block of code that you can use again.
A name in a function definition that receives a value.
The real value you give a function when you call it.
The result a function sends back to the code that called it.
Code that repeats.
A test that is true or false, used by if and while.
A note in the code that Python ignores. It explains why.
Text in triple quotes at the start of a function that says what it does.
A file of Python code that you can import and use.
Code that other people wrote, which you can use in your own program.
A plan for making objects that have data and actions.
A thing made from a class. It has its own data.
A function that belongs to an object or class.
An error that stops the program unless you catch it.
The list of lines that led to an error. Read it from the bottom.
A mistake in the code.
To find and fix bugs.
A small check that says what the output should be for an input.
An unusual input, such as an empty list, that often breaks code.
A run that shows what would happen but changes nothing.
A service made for programs to use, often returning JSON.
A text format for data, made of dictionaries and lists.
A table saved as plain text, with commas between the columns.
A short fingerprint of some content. The same content gives the same hash.
A setting stored outside your code, good for keeping secrets such as keys.
A project folder that Git tracks. Also called a repo.
A saved step in the history of a project, with a short message.
The text you send to an AI model.
A small piece of text that an AI model reads. Often a short word or part of a word.
The manual that explains how a tool or library works. Short for documentation.
A group of values that cannot be changed, written with round brackets.
A group of unique values with no order, written with curly brackets.
Putting each value of a tuple or list into its own name, like x, y = point.
A small function written in one line, with no name.
A function that tells sorted or max which value to compare.
The modules that come with Python, such as math, csv and json.
A statement that brings a module into your program.
A pattern for finding text, such as \d+ for digits. Also called a regex.
A string that starts with r. Backslashes in it are kept as they are.
In a regular expression, a part in round brackets whose match you can read separately.
When a function calls itself to solve a smaller version of the problem.
The case in a recursive function that stops without calling itself again.
Saving the results of function calls so the same work is not done twice.
A class that mainly holds data, with __init__ and __repr__ written for you.
A note about the expected type, like x: int. Python does not check it.
An object used with "with" that does setup and cleanup for you.
A function that gives values one at a time with yield.
A function that wraps another function to add behaviour, used with @.
An object that gives its items one by one when you loop over it.
A short way to build a list from a loop, like [n * 2 for n in numbers].
A string that starts with f and puts values inside curly brackets.
Part of a list or string, like items[1:3].
The position of an item in a list or string, counting from 0.
Can be changed after it is made, like a list.
Cannot be changed after it is made, like a tuple or a string.
A special value that means "nothing is here".
The value a parameter gets when you do not give one.
An argument given by name, like greet(name="Sam").
The spaces at the start of a line that show which block it belongs to.
An error because Python cannot read the code, such as a missing colon.
A variable that belongs to an object.
Making a new class that gets everything from another class and adds more.
The name a method gives to the object it is working on.
A list of steps that solves a problem.
The tool that installs Python packages.
The front page of a project. It says what it is and how to run it.
A simple way to format text with symbols like # and -.
A tool that keeps the history of a project.
A website that stores Git projects online.
Sending your commits to GitHub.
